a: The LORD says this:
p: Chapters 56–66 open here. Most scholars call them Third Isaiah; the messenger formula marks a new word.
b: Koh amar YHWH, "The LORD says this", is the formula of a messenger who repeats his master's words exactly; this site renders it the same way everywhere (first in Isaiah at 7:7). Here it opens the last part of the book. Since Bernhard Duhm (1892) most critical scholars have called chapters 56–66 "Third Isaiah" (Trito-Isaiah), words of prophets in Judah after the return from Babylon in 538 BC; those who hold to one Isaiah read them as the prophet of Jerusalem looking ahead to that time (see book.json and the settings below). One numbering note for this part: English 64:1 is the last half of Hebrew 63:19, and English 64:2–12 are Hebrew 64:1–11. This site uses the English numbers throughout.

a: Keep justice and practice righteousness
p: The people are to do tsedaqah, because God's own tsedaqah is about to appear. One word, two senses.
b: Mishpat and tsedaqah, "justice and righteousness", are the prophets' pair for fair dealing (5:7). But in Isaiah 40–66 God's tsedaqah often means his saving action: his victory, rescue or vindication of his people (46:13; 51:5–6). This verse puts the two senses side by side: "practice righteousness... and my righteousness to being revealed." The Plain keeps one English word for both so the play shows. The verse sums up a turn many scholars see in these chapters: the promises of 40–55 still stand, but now they wait on a people who act justly (compare 59:9–15).

a: Happy is the mortal who does this
p: The blessing formula of Psalm 1 opens the welcome of outsiders.
b: Ashre, "Happy", is the opening word of the Psalms (Psalm 1:1) and of Psalm 119. The pair enosh and ben adam, "mortal" and "human being", is general on purpose: the blessing is not limited to Israelites by birth. The next verses show who is meant, foreigners and eunuchs. Two signs mark them: keeping the Sabbath and keeping one's hand from evil. Sabbath-keeping was one of the marks of a Jew in exile, where temple and land were gone (compare Ezekiel 20:12; Nehemiah 13:15–22).

a: The foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD
p: The law kept some foreigners out of the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3–8). Isaiah says a foreigner joined to the LORD belongs.
b: Ben hannekhar, "son of foreignness", is a person of non-Israelite birth; nilvah, "joined", is the word Zechariah uses for nations who "will join themselves to the LORD" (Zechariah 2:11; compare Isaiah 14:1). Deuteronomy 23:3–8 kept Ammonites and Moabites out of the LORD's assembly, and Ezra and Nehemiah enforced it by sending away foreign wives (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:1–3). Isaiah 56 sets a different emphasis: the test is loyalty to the LORD, his Sabbath and his covenant, not ancestry. Scholars debate whether the two stand in tension (Blenkinsopp, Hanson) or answer different situations: Ezra's mixed marriages with people who kept their own gods, and here foreigners who have taken the LORD as God. Later Jewish tradition read the verse of converts (Rashi, Kimchi).

a: I am a dried-up tree
p: A man who had been castrated could have no children, and the law barred him from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1).
b: Saris means a eunuch, a castrated man, and also a court official, since kings often used eunuchs to serve in the palace (2 Kings 20:18 warned that Hezekiah's descendants would become eunuchs in Babylon's palace; compare Daniel 1:3). Here the meaning is physical: the man calls himself a "dried-up tree", one who will bear no fruit, no children to carry his name. Deuteronomy 23:1 barred a man with crushed or cut-off genitals from the LORD's assembly. Isaiah does not cancel that law in so many words, but he promises such men a place "in my house". Acts 8:26–39 tells of an Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah and being baptized, and many readers have seen this chapter fulfilled in him.

a: a marker and a name
p: Yad means "hand", here a standing stone or monument. Israel's Holocaust memorial takes its name from this verse.
b: Yad vashem, literally "a hand and a name". Yad can mean a monument: Absalom, who had no son, set up a pillar and called it "Absalom's hand" so his name would be remembered (2 Samuel 18:18). A man without children feared his name would die with him; God promises the eunuch a lasting memorial "in my house and inside my walls", better than sons and daughters. The phrase gave its name to Yad Vashem, Israel's memorial to the Jews killed in the Holocaust, set up in Jerusalem by a law of 1953, many of whose victims left no one to carry their names.

a: to minister to him
p: Sharet is the word for the service of priests and Levites. Foreigners are pictured serving in the temple.
b: Lesharto, "to minister to him", is the verb for temple service by priests and Levites (Deuteronomy 10:8; Ezekiel 44:11). Ezekiel 44:6–9 had condemned letting foreigners serve in the sanctuary. Isaiah 56 pictures foreigners loving the LORD's name, keeping his covenant and offering acceptable sacrifices. The book ends by going further: God will take some from the nations "to be Levite priests" (66:21). The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks "to minister to him" and "to love" here (see the variant), which some read as a scribe softening the claim.

a: a house of prayer for all the peoples
p: Jesus quoted this line when he drove the traders out of the temple (Mark 11:17), joined to Jeremiah 7:11.
b: In Mark 11:17 Jesus says, "Is it not written, 'My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a hideout for robbers" (Jeremiah 7:11). Mark quotes the Greek of Isaiah, which matches the Hebrew here, and only Mark keeps "for all the nations"; Matthew 21:13 and Luke 19:46 stop at "house of prayer". The trading took place in the outer court, the one part of Herod's temple where non-Jews could pray, so the full line sharpens the protest. Solomon's prayer had already asked God to hear the foreigner who prays toward the temple (1 Kings 8:41–43).
r: Mark 11:17; Matthew 21:13; Luke 19:46; Jeremiah 7:11; 1 Kings 8:41–43; John 2:16

a: the banished of Israel
p: God gathers Israel's exiles and promises to gather still others. Jesus' "other sheep" may echo it.
b: Nidche Yisra'el, "the banished of Israel", are the exiles driven out of the land (11:12; Deuteronomy 30:4; Psalm 147:2). "Still more I will gather to him" most naturally means the foreigners of 56:3–7, added to the returning exiles. Many readers hear an echo in Jesus' words, "I also have other sheep, ones that do not belong to this courtyard. I must lead those as well" (John 10:16), and in the gathering of the nations at the book's end (66:18–21). The Jewish daily Amidah blesses God "who gathers the banished of his people Israel", using this phrase.

a: Its watchmen are blind
p: The leaders who should warn the people are blind, and the guard dogs cannot bark.
b: A tsofeh, "watchman", stood on the wall to warn of danger; the prophets used the word for themselves (Ezekiel 3:17; Ezekiel 33:7; Habakkuk 2:1). Here the watchmen are the people's leaders, prophets or rulers, and they are blind and mute, like sheepdogs that sleep and cannot bark. In 56:11 they are also greedy dogs and shepherds. The scene opens a long charge against Judah's leaders and worshipers that runs to 57:13. "Its watchmen" means Israel's, or Jerusalem's; the Hebrew has a Ketiv-Qere here: the written text reads "they have watched", and the reading tradition "its watchmen" (see the topic ketiv-qere).

a: And these are the shepherds!
p: Ro'im means "shepherds". The Greek read the same letters as "wicked".
b: The Hebrew consonants r'ym can be read ro'im, "shepherds", or ra'im, "evil ones". The Masoretes read "shepherds", and the Great Isaiah Scroll writes it with the article, "the shepherds"; the Greek has poneroi, "wicked". Kings and leaders were called shepherds across the ancient Near East (Ezekiel 34:2–10; Jeremiah 23:1–4). The irony is sharp: the shepherds who should care for the flock are themselves like hungry dogs, "each after his own profit".

a: let us swill beer
p: The leaders' party song recalls the drinkers of 5:11–12 and 22:13.
b: Shekar is beer, mostly made from grain (the site's rendering everywhere; "strong drink" in older versions). The leaders' song, "Tomorrow will be just like today", is the opposite of the feast in 22:13, "Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die": they think tomorrow will bring only more of the same. Isaiah of Jerusalem had already condemned leaders who drink while the people perish (5:11–12, 22; 28:7). The Greek has no 56:12 at all (see the variant).

a: The righteous one perishes
p: The righteous die and no one notices. Jewish readers took it as mercy; Justin read it of Christ.
b: The Hebrew can mean the righteous are taken away "from the presence of evil", that is, spared from the disaster to come, or "because of evil", killed by the wicked. The first reading has a model in Huldah's word to Josiah: "You will be gathered into your grave in peace, and your eyes will not have to see all the disaster" (2 Kings 22:20). Rashi and Kimchi read it that way, and the saying that the righteous are taken before a calamity became proverbial in Jewish tradition. Justin Martyr read 57:1 of the death of Jesus, "the Righteous One", whom no one took to heart (Dialogue with Trypho 16). In context the verse begins the charge against a people who do not care when good people die.

a: rest on their beds
p: Mishkav, "bed", is also a word for a burial place. The righteous rest in death.
b: Mishkav is the ordinary word for a bed, but it is also used of a tomb (Ezekiel 32:25; 2 Chronicles 16:14, where Asa is laid "on a bed"). So the dead righteous "go into peace" and lie at rest. The same word comes back with a very different sense in 57:7–8, where the people's "bed" is the place of their idolatry and adultery. The contrast seems intended.

a: you sons of a fortune-teller
p: An 'onenah read omens. Calling the people her children is an insult: their real parent is their false religion.
b: 'Onenah is a woman who practices 'onen, reading signs or casting spells, one of the arts the law forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10; 2 Kings 21:6, of Manasseh). "Offspring of an adulterer and of a woman who plays the prostitute" uses the prophets' picture of idolatry as unfaithfulness in marriage (Hosea 2:2–5; Jeremiah 3:6–9; Ezekiel 16). The prophet says nothing literal about the hearers' mothers. He says they are true children of a people who went after other gods.

a: among the great trees
p: 'Elim may be "oaks" or "gods". Worship under green trees was the hallmark of the high places.
b: Ba'elim can mean "among the oaks" or "terebinths" (as in 1:29, "you will be ashamed of the oaks you wanted") or "with the gods"; the Greek, Targum and Vulgate took it as "idols". "Under every leafy tree" is the stock phrase for the hill shrines of Canaanite worship (Deuteronomy 12:2; 1 Kings 14:23; 2 Kings 16:4; Jeremiah 2:20). The "lust" may be literal ritual sex, or the prophets' picture of idolatry as adultery, or both.

a: You slaughter children in the ravines
p: Children were killed as offerings in valleys like the Valley of Hinnom below Jerusalem.
b: The law forbids making children "pass through the fire" (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 18:10). Kings Ahaz and Manasseh did it (2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6), and Jeremiah condemned the shrine of Topheth "in the Valley of Ben-hinnom", where children were burned (Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 19:5). Josiah destroyed it (2 Kings 23:10). That this rite is charged here has led some scholars to date 57:3–13 before the exile; others think such practices survived among those left in the land, or that the prophet uses the old sins to describe the present. The same valley later gave its name to Gehenna, the place of final punishment (see 66:24).
r: Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 19:5; Ezekiel 16:20–21; 66:24

a: Among the smooth stones of the ravine is your share
p: Chalqe, "smooth things", sounds like chelqekh, "your share". The people chose stones as their inheritance.
b: The line is a pun: bechalqe nachal chelqekh, "among the smooth ones of the ravine is your portion". Israel's true "portion" was the LORD himself (Psalm 16:5; Jeremiah 10:16), and the Levites had no land because "The LORD is their inheritance" (Deuteronomy 18:2). Here the people have chosen sacred stones in the valleys instead. What the "smooth ones" were is debated: standing stones used as idols, stones set up over the dead, or, as William Irwin argued from the related Ugaritic word, the dead themselves, honored in the valley. "Should I be content with these things?" uses nacham, the verb for being comforted or changing one's mind.

a: Behind the door and the doorpost
p: Israel was to write God's words on the doorpost (mezuzah). Here an idol's "reminder" hides behind it.
b: Mezuzah, "doorpost", is the place where Deuteronomy commands Israel to write the LORD's words (Deuteronomy 6:9; Deuteronomy 11:20), the origin of the small scroll Jews still fix to their doorposts. Here the people have set up a zikkaron, a "reminder" or memorial, of another kind behind the door: a sign or image of another god. The rest of the verse uses the language of sex. "Uncovered your bed" and "made it wide" picture a wife inviting lovers, and "you gazed on a hand" likely uses yad, "hand", as a polite word for the male organ, as it is in some other ancient texts. The prophet's point is betrayal, said as bluntly as the Hebrew allows.
orig: וְאַחַר הַדֶּלֶת וְהַמְּזוּזָה שַׂמְתְּ זִכְרוֹנֵךְ (ve'achar haddelet vehammezuzah samt zikhronekh)

a: You went down to the king with oil
p: Melekh means "king". Many read it as the god Molech, whose name has the same letters.
b: The consonants mlk spell melekh, "king", and also the name the Hebrew Bible gives the god of child sacrifice, Molech (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10). Since 57:5 has just mentioned slaughtered children, and since the verse goes on to envoys sent "down as deep as Sheol", many scholars hear a reference to Molech, perhaps a god of the dead. Others take "the king" as a foreign ruler, Assyrian or Persian, courted with gifts of oil and perfume, as Hosea 12:1 says Israel "carries oil to Egypt". The Plain keeps the plain meaning "king" and leaves the other reading here.

a: let your collection save you!
p: Qibbutsayikh, "your collections", is a mocking word for a heap of idols.
b: Qibbutsayikh means "your gatherings" or "your collection". It may mean a crowd of gods or idols gathered over time, or the allies and helpers the people had collected. The point is the same as the idol satire of 44:9–20: what you heaped together will not save you, and a puff of wind will carry it off. The word hevel, "breath", is Ecclesiastes' "vapor" ("Vapor of vapors", Ecclesiastes 1:2).

a: will receive the land as an inheritance
p: The promise of the land goes to the one who takes refuge in the LORD. Psalm 37 and Jesus say the same.
b: The pairing of nachal "inherit" and yarash "possess" goes back to the promise of Canaan. Here the condition is trust: "the one who shelters in me". Psalm 37:9–11 promises that those who wait for the LORD and "the humble will take possession of the land" (Psalm 37:11), and Jesus took up the same words: "Blessed are the gentle, because they will inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5). In 65:9 the heirs of the LORD's mountains are "my chosen ones".

a: Heap it up, heap it up, clear the way!
p: The road-building call of 40:3 returns, now to clear stumbling blocks from God's people.
b: Sollu sollu, "heap it up, heap it up", is the work of piling earth to make a raised road. In 40:3 a voice called for a highway for God through the desert; in 62:10 the same words recur at the gates of Zion. Here the road is cleared of mikhshol, a "stumbling block": the obstacles in the way are now the people's own sins. The synagogue reads 57:14–58:14 as the prophetic reading on the morning of the Day of Atonement, a custom already known to the Talmud (Bavli Megillah 31a), because of the call to true repentance and fasting in chapter 58.

a: the One who lives for all time
p: The KJV's "inhabiteth eternity" is famous. The Hebrew says God dwells, or sits enthroned, forever.
b: Shokhen 'ad is literally "dwelling (for) perpetuity". The KJV's "the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity" made it sound as if eternity were a place where God lives. Most scholars take 'ad as an adverb, "forever", so God "dwells forever" or "is enthroned forever"; the Plain has "lives for all time", though the phrase may also hint at "inhabiting" timelessness. "High and lifted up" is the description of the LORD on his throne in Isaiah's vision (6:1) and of the servant raised high (52:13). The surprise comes next: the God who is so high also lives "with the crushed and the lowly in spirit".

a: and with the crushed and the lowly in spirit
p: The highest God lives with the lowest people. Psalm 51 and Jesus' first beatitude say the same.
b: Dakka', "crushed", is the word of Psalm 34:18, "he saves those whose spirits are crushed", and of Psalm 51:17, "A heart broken and crushed". The servant of 53:5 and 53:10 is "crushed" with the same root. Jesus' blessing on "those who are poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3) stands in this tradition, as does 66:2, where God looks to "the poor one, stricken in spirit". In Jewish tradition the verse is a key text for the humility of God, who lowers himself to dwell with the humble (Bavli Megillah 31a cites it).

a: I will not go on suing forever
p: God's case against his people will not last forever, because he made their breath.
b: Riv is a lawsuit or quarrel, the word of the prophets' covenant lawsuits (3:13; Micah 6:2). Psalm 103:9 says the same: "He will not go on accusing without end." The reason given is God's care for what he made: the neshamot, "breaths", are the breath of life God blew into the first human (Genesis 2:7). If his anger went on, the creatures he made would faint away. The Greek reads "for spirit will go out from me, and I have made all breath".

a: I am the one who creates the fruit of lips
p: God creates words of praise and peace. Hebrews 13:15 calls praise "the fruit of lips".
b: Niv sefatayim, "fruit of lips", is speech, here the thanks or the greeting of peace that God himself makes possible. Hebrews 13:15 urges Christians to offer God "a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name", drawing on this verse and the Greek of Hosea 14:2. The word niv has a Ketiv-Qere: the written text has nuv, the reading tradition niv; both mean "fruit".

a: 'Peace, peace, to the one who is far and the one who is near,'
p: Paul hears gentiles (far) and Jews (near) in this line. The rabbis heard repentant sinners and the righteous.
b: In the context the "far" are the exiles still scattered and the "near" those in Judah. Paul applies the verse to Christ: "he came and announced the good news of peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near" (Ephesians 2:17), the gentiles and the Jews, made one people (Ephesians 2:13–18). The rabbis noticed that the far one is named first and drew a famous lesson: "In the place where those who repent stand, the completely righteous cannot stand" (Bavli Berakhot 34b), the far being the one who has come back.

a: "The wicked have no peace," says my God.
t: A refrain that divides the book
p: The same line closes 48:22. With 66:24, it marks three groups of nine chapters in 40–66.
b: This verse repeats 48:22 almost word for word, with "my God" for "the LORD", and the Plain uses the same wording. Nineteenth-century scholars such as Franz Delitzsch noticed that the refrain closes chapters 48 and 57, and that 66:24 ends the book on a similar note, so that chapters 40–66 fall into three sets of nine. The structure is admired by many commentators, though not all think it was planned. Here the line answers 57:19: peace is offered far and near, but the wicked, who are like a churning sea (57:20), will not have it.

a: Lift your voice like a ram's horn!
p: The shofar, a ram's horn trumpet, called Israel to war, to feasts and to repentance.
b: The shofar was a curved ram's horn blown to sound an alarm (Hosea 8:1; Amos 3:6), to call an assembly (Joel 2:15, "Blow the ram's horn in Zion, call a fast") and to announce the Jubilee on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 25:9). Here the prophet himself is to be the horn. The connection with fasting and the Day of Atonement fits the chapter, and it is one reason the synagogue reads this chapter on that day, when the shofar is also sounded at its close.

a: as if they were a nation that practiced righteousness
p: The people seek God daily and want his rulings. The trouble is not too little religion.
b: The irony is heavy. Every phrase is good: seeking God, wanting to know his ways, asking for righteous rulings, wanting to come near. The people are like a nation that does what is right. That "like" is the charge: the outward forms are there, but the justice that should go with them is not (58:3–4). Prophets before the exile made the same complaint about sacrifices (1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24; Micah 6:6–8). After the exile the complaint is about fasting, the chief act of piety left when the temple was in ruins.

a: Why did we humble ourselves, and you did not notice?
p: "Afflict our souls" is the law's phrase for the Day of Atonement fast.
b: 'Innu nafshenu, "we humbled our selves", is the phrase the law uses for the fast of the Day of Atonement: "you must humble yourselves" (Leviticus 16:29, 31; Leviticus 23:27). This site renders it "humble yourselves" everywhere. After the fall of Jerusalem the people also kept fasts of mourning in the fifth and seventh months, and in the days of Darius they asked whether they should go on (Zechariah 7:3–5; Zechariah 8:19). God's answer through Zechariah is close to Isaiah 58: "Judge with true justice, and show loyal love and mercy to one another" (Zechariah 7:9).
r: Leviticus 16:29; Leviticus 16:31; Leviticus 23:27; Zechariah 7:3–10; Zechariah 8:19; Psalm 35:13

a: you go after your own business
p: Chefets is "pleasure" and also "business, affairs". The same word returns in the Sabbath verse, 58:13.
b: Chefets means what one wants: delight, or the affairs one pursues, as in "every matter under the heavens has its time" (Ecclesiastes 3:1). The KJV took it as "pleasure". In context it seems to mean business: on the very day they fast, the people carry on their trade and "drive all your workers hard", using the verb of Egypt's slave drivers (nagas, Exodus 3:7; Exodus 5:6). 58:13 uses the same word twice: true Sabbath-keeping means turning back "from doing your own business on my holy day".

a: hangs his head like a bulrush
p: Bowed heads, sackcloth and ashes were the outward signs of fasting and grief.
b: An 'agmon is a reed or bulrush, whose head droops. Sackcloth was rough goats' hair cloth worn against the skin, and ashes were thrown on the head or spread to lie on (Esther 4:3; Jonah 3:6; Daniel 9:3). God does not condemn these signs as such. Joel calls for fasting and weeping (Joel 2:12), and Nineveh's sackcloth was accepted (Jonah 3:10). The question is whether the bowing of the head goes with a changed life. Jesus warned against fasting "to be seen" (Matthew 6:16–18).

a: to send the crushed away free
t: A line Jesus read in Nazareth
p: Luke 4:18 slips this line, in its Greek form, into Jesus' reading of Isaiah 61.
b: Shallach retsutsim chofshim, "to send the crushed away free", uses chofshi, the word for a slave set free (Exodus 21:2; Jeremiah 34:9–10). In Jeremiah's day the people freed their Hebrew slaves and then took them back (Jeremiah 34:8–17); the true fast undoes such wrongs. When Jesus reads Isaiah in the Nazareth synagogue, Luke's quotation of 61:1–2 includes this line from the Greek of 58:6, "to send the crushed away free" (Luke 4:18). Scholars debate whether Luke combined the texts or the synagogue reading did; either way it ties the true fast to Jesus' mission.

a: Is it not to break your bread for the hungry
p: Feeding the hungry, sheltering the uprooted and clothing the naked: Jesus' judgment scene uses the same list.
b: Paros, "break", is the breaking of a flat loaf to share it (Lamentations 4:4). The list, food for the hungry, a roof for the afflicted and uprooted (merudim, people driven from home) and clothes for the naked, is the core of what later Judaism called gemilut chasadim, acts of loyal love, and of the Christian "works of mercy". Ezekiel names the same acts as the marks of a righteous man (Ezekiel 18:7, 16), and Jesus makes them the test in the judgment of the nations (Matthew 25:35–36). "Your own flesh and blood" (literally "your own flesh") means one's relatives and, more widely, every fellow human being.
orig: הֲלוֹא פָרֹס לָרָעֵב לַחְמֶךָ (halo' faros lara'ev lachmekha)
r: Ezekiel 18:7; Ezekiel 18:16; Job 31:16–20; Matthew 25:35–36; James 2:15–16; Genesis 29:14

a: the LORD's glory will gather you in from behind
p: As at the exodus, God goes before and behind his people. The verb is the word for a rear guard.
b: Ya'asfekha, "will gather you", is the verb of the me'assef, the rear guard that gathers stragglers at the back of a marching column (Numbers 10:25; Joshua 6:9). In 52:12 God promised the exiles, "the God of Israel will be your rear guard", and both passages recall the pillar of cloud that moved behind Israel at the sea (Exodus 14:19–20). Here righteousness marches ahead and God's glory follows behind: the people who act justly are surrounded by God's presence.

a: he will say, "I am here."
p: Hinneni, "Here I am", is what Abraham, Samuel and Isaiah said to God. Now God says it to his people.
b: Hinneni is the answer of a servant ready to obey: Abraham's "Here I am" (Genesis 22:1, 11), Samuel's (1 Samuel 3:4), and Isaiah's own "Here I am, send me" (6:8). In 58:9 God himself gives that answer to people who call on him after they have done justice. In 65:1 God says "I am here, I am here" to a nation that did not even call. The Greek adds, "while you are still speaking, he will say, Here I am", which echoes 65:24.

a: the jabbing finger
p: A pointing finger was a gesture of scorn or accusation, perhaps of a curse.
b: Shelach etsba', "sending out the finger", is pointing at someone in contempt, as the worthless man of Proverbs 6:13 "points with his fingers". It may also be a gesture that went with a curse or a false charge in court. Joined with "the wicked word", it covers the ways the strong put down the weak: scorn, gossip, false accusation. These, with the "yoke" of oppression, are what the true fast removes.

a: if you offer your own self to the hungry
p: Nefesh is throat, appetite, life, self. Give your nefesh to the hungry, and fill the hungry nefesh.
b: Nefesh often means the hungry throat or appetite (5:14; Proverbs 27:7), and also a person's very life or self. The verse plays on both: "if you offer your nefesh to the hungry and satisfy the nefesh of the afflicted". The giver gives not just bread but himself, and in return the LORD will "fill your hunger" (literally "satisfy your nefesh") in the scorched lands (58:11). The Greek reads "give your bread from your soul" (see the variant).

a: whose waters do not lie
t: A spring that does not lie
p: A wadi that runs dry in summer "lies". God's people will be a spring that never fails.
b: Kazav is "to lie, deceive". In the dry lands of Judah, a wadi full in winter disappoints the traveler in summer; Jeremiah complains to God, "Will you be to me like a deceptive brook, like waters that fail?" (Jeremiah 15:18). Here the people who care for the hungry become a garden "soaked with water" and a spring whose water does not lie, a source for others. Jesus' promise of a spring welling up to eternal life (John 4:14; John 7:38) draws on images like this.

a: the Mender of the Gap in the Wall
p: After the exile Jerusalem's walls lay broken for decades until Nehemiah rebuilt them (445 BC).
b: Goder perets, "one who walls up a breach", is the builder who closes a gap knocked in a city wall; the KJV made "repairer of the breach" a well-known phrase. After Babylon broke down Jerusalem's walls in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:10), the gaps stood open until Nehemiah's rebuilding about 445 BC (Nehemiah 2:13–17; Nehemiah 6:1). Ezekiel had blamed the prophets who did not "go up into the breaches" (Ezekiel 13:5; Ezekiel 22:30). Isaiah promises that people who do justice will be the ones to rebuild, a moral as well as a physical repair.

a: if you call the Sabbath a delight
p: "Sabbath delight" became a Jewish name for the joy of the day, with good food, rest and study.
b: 'Oneg, "delight", is the root of 58:14's "the LORD will be your delight". The rabbis took the phrase as a command to honor the Sabbath with pleasure: special meals, clean clothes, rest (Bavli Shabbat 118a–b). From "talking on and on" (literally "speaking a word") they drew the rule that "your speech on the Sabbath should not be like your weekday speech" (Bavli Shabbat 113a–b). Modern Jews still call a Friday evening gathering an Oneg Shabbat. The verse joins the Sabbath to the justice of 58:6–10: the same "business" that oppressed workers on the fast (58:3) must stop on the Sabbath.

a: and I will set you riding over the land's high places
t: Words from the Song of Moses
p: This is a quotation of Deuteronomy 32:13, from the Song of Moses.
b: Deuteronomy 32:13 says of Israel in the wilderness, "He set him riding over the land's high places, / and he fed on what the fields grew" (Deuteronomy 32:13). Isaiah reuses the line, and the Plain gives it the same words because the Hebrew is the same. Here the "high places" are the hill country, not shrines. The promise is for the people who keep the Sabbath: they will have the land again as Jacob's inheritance. The rabbis noticed that Jacob's blessing had no boundaries, "you will break out westward and eastward, northward and southward" (Genesis 28:14), and said that whoever delights in the Sabbath receives "an inheritance without limits" (Bavli Shabbat 118a). "The mouth of the LORD has spoken" seals the promise, as in 1:20 and 40:5.

a: the LORD's hand has not grown too short to save
p: "Is the LORD's hand too short?" God asked Moses in the wilderness. The answer is still no.
b: A "short hand" is a weak one, unable to reach or act. God asked Moses, "Is the LORD's hand too short?" when Moses doubted he could feed Israel meat (Numbers 11:23), and in 50:2 God asked the exiles, "Is my hand too short to redeem?" Here the prophet answers the people's complaint that God does not save or listen. The problem is not God's power or his hearing. It is the people's sin (59:2).

a: No, it is your wrongdoings that have split you off from your God
p: Badal, "separate", is the verb the foreigner feared in 56:3. Now sin, not birth, is what separates.
b: Mavdilim, "separating", is from badal, the word for dividing light from darkness (Genesis 1:4), Israel from the nations (Leviticus 20:24) and the holy from the common. In 56:3 the foreigner feared that the LORD would "separate" him from his people. In 59:2 the only thing that separates anyone from God is wrongdoing. "Hidden his face" is the opposite of the priestly blessing, "May the LORD make his face shine toward you" (Numbers 6:25); compare 1:15, "I will hide my eyes from you".

a: No one sues for what is right
p: Qore' means one who "calls" or summons, here a person who brings a case to court.
b: The verse speaks the language of the town gate, where elders heard cases (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–11; Amos 5:10–15). Qore' betsedeq, "one who calls in righteousness", is a plaintiff who brings an honest suit; nishpat be'emunah is one who goes to judgment truthfully. No one does either. The images of 59:5–6 then describe what the schemers produce: viper's eggs that kill whoever eats them, and spider's webs too thin to make a garment.

a: Their feet run to evil
p: Romans 3:15–17 uses these lines, in the Greek wording, in Paul's chain of texts showing that all have sinned.
b: In Romans 3:10–18 Paul strings together verses from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that "all, Jews and Greeks, are under sin" (Romans 3:9). Romans 3:15–17 is a shortened form of 59:7–8 in the Greek: "Their feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery are in their paths, and the way of peace they have not known." Isaiah spoke of Judah's own leaders and people, and Paul's point is the same: the people who had God's law are not exempt. Proverbs 1:16 has almost the same words as 59:7.

a: That is why justice is far from us
p: From here the speakers are "we". The people take up the prophet's charge as their own confession.
b: The voice changes from "you" (59:1–8) to "we". Whether the prophet speaks for the people or a group among them prays, the words turn into a lament and then a confession (59:12–13). Mishpat and tsedaqah here mean the justice and saving help that God gives: the people wait for him to set things right, but their own injustice keeps it away. The light they hope for is the light promised in 58:8 and 58:10, and given in 60:1.
orig: עַל־כֵּן רָחַק מִשְׁפָּט מִמֶּנּוּ ('al-ken rachaq mishpat mimmennu)

a: Among the hale and hearty we are like the dead
p: 'Ashmannim occurs only here. It may mean "the vigorous", "dark places" or "desolate places".
b: Ba'ashmannim is found nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Some connect it with shamen, "fat, robust", hence "among the stout" or "the vigorous" (the reading of many modern versions, and of the Plain). Others think of the dark: "in dark places like the dead" (compare Lamentations 3:6). The Targum and Rashi understood "in desolate places". The KJV's "we are in desolate places as dead men" follows that line. The sense either way is that the people are as good as dead while everyone else seems alive.

a: For our rebellions before you are many
p: After the exile, public confession of sin became a form of prayer: Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9, Daniel 9.
b: Israel's prayers after the exile often confess the sins of the nation as "our" sins, even when the speaker is personally faithful: Ezra (Ezra 9:6–15), the Levites (Nehemiah 9:16–37) and Daniel (Daniel 9:4–19). 59:12–13 uses the same three words for sin the law uses on the Day of Atonement, pesha' "rebellion", chatta't "sin" and 'avon "wrongdoing" (Leviticus 16:21). Such confession was the first step back to God (Leviticus 26:40–42).
r: Ezra 9:6–15; Nehemiah 9:16–37; Daniel 9:4–19; Leviticus 16:21; Leviticus 26:40–42; Psalm 51:3

a: he was shocked that no one stepped in
p: Mafgia' is one who steps in between, an intercessor. The servant of 53:12 was one.
b: Mafgia', from paga' "meet, intercede", is one who comes between to plead or to act. The servant of 53:12 "will step in for the rebels", with the same verb, and Jeremiah was told not to "intercede" for the people (Jeremiah 7:16). Finding no human helper, God acts himself: "his own arm brought him victory". The same words return in 63:5, where the warrior comes from Edom. Ezekiel 22:30 makes the same complaint: God looked for someone to "stand in the gap" and found no one.
orig: וַיִּשְׁתּוֹמֵם כִּי אֵין מַפְגִּיעַ (vayyishtomem ki 'en mafgia')

a: Righteousness he wore as his armor
p: God dresses for battle in righteousness and salvation. Paul gives the same armor to believers.
b: The LORD arms himself like a warrior: shiryon is scale armor for the body, and kova' a helmet. His armor is his own righteousness, salvation, vengeance and zeal. The Wisdom of Solomon (5:17–20) develops the picture. Paul turns it into the believer's equipment: "the breastplate of righteousness" and "the helmet of salvation" (Ephesians 6:14, 17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8). Isaiah's warrior wears these as the one who fights; in Paul, God's people put on his armor to stand firm.

a: For he will come like a river in a narrow channel
t: "When the enemy comes in like a flood"
p: The KJV's famous line reads the same words differently: the enemy comes like a flood, and the Spirit raises a standard.
b: The KJV reads, "When the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him." That takes tsar as "enemy" and nosesah as "raise a banner" (from nes, "banner"). Most modern scholars read tsar as "narrow", describing a river forced through a tight channel, and nosesah as "drives on", from nasas; the coming one is the LORD himself, rushing like a pent-up flood driven by his wind (ruach, also "spirit"). Both readings are possible from the letters. The KJV wording has a long life in preaching and hymns, and the medieval Jewish commentators already argued over it.
orig: כִּי־יָבוֹא כַנָּהָר צָר רוּחַ יְהוָה נֹסְסָה בוֹ (ki-yavo' khannahar tsar ruach YHWH nosesah vo)

a: "A redeemer will come to Zion,
p: Paul quotes 59:20–21 in Romans 11:26–27, from the Greek, with "from Zion" and "turn away ungodliness from Jacob".
b: Paul writes, "and in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written: 'The Deliverer will come out of Zion; he will turn ungodliness away from Jacob. And this is my covenant with them, when I take away their sins'" (Romans 11:26–27). The Hebrew has "to Zion" and "to those in Jacob who turn from rebellion"; the Greek has "for the sake of Zion" and "he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob"; Paul has "out of Zion", perhaps from Psalm 14:7, and adds a line from 27:9. In the Hebrew the people's repentance comes first; in the Greek and in Paul, the Deliverer brings it about. See the variant.

a: redeemer
p: A go'el was the relative who bought back family members or land. Isaiah gives God the title.
b: The go'el was the next of kin who redeemed a relative sold into slavery or land lost to debt (Leviticus 25:25, 47–49), as Boaz did for Ruth (Ruth 4). Isaiah 40–66 calls God Israel's go'el again and again (41:14; 43:14; 44:6; 49:7; 54:5; 60:16; 63:16). This site renders it "redeemer" when the go'el is God. Jewish tradition reads 59:20 of the Messiah (the Targum has "the redeemer", and the verse opens the daily prayer U-va le-Tsiyyon go'el), and Christians read it of Christ.

a: "As for me, this is my covenant with them," says the LORD.
t: A covenant of spirit and word
p: God promises that his spirit and words will never leave "your" mouth. Who is "you"?
b: The verse is prose and changes from "them" to "you" (singular). "You" may be the people as a whole, now given the prophetic spirit (compare Joel 2:28–29; Numbers 11:29); the prophet himself and those who carry on his words (compare 61:1, "the Spirit of the Lord GOD is on me"); or the servant of 42:1 and 49:2, whose mouth God made like a sword. The promise of words that "will not leave your mouth" echoes Joshua 1:8 on the book of the law. The verse, with 59:20, opens the Jewish prayer U-va le-Tsiyyon, said daily, and Christians have read it of the Spirit given to the church (Acts 2:17–18, 39).

a: Rise up and shine, for your light has come
p: The Hebrew verbs are feminine: Zion is addressed as a woman, as in 51:17 and 52:1–2.
b: Qumi 'ori, "rise, shine", are feminine singular commands. The city is addressed as a woman sitting in the dust of mourning, as in 52:2 ("Shake the dust off; rise and sit, Jerusalem") and 51:17. Now her light has come. The LORD's glory "has dawned" (zarach, the verb for sunrise) over her, the way the LORD "dawned from Seir" at Sinai (Deuteronomy 33:2). The glory that left the temple in Ezekiel's vision (Ezekiel 10–11) returns (Ezekiel 43:1–5). Handel joined this verse to 40:9 in the aria "O thou that tellest good tidings to Zion", and set 60:2–3 as the recitative that follows it.

a: Nations will walk toward your light
p: The vision of 2:2–5 returns. Revelation 21:24 takes it up for the new Jerusalem.
b: In 2:3–5 the nations stream to the mountain of the LORD, and Israel is invited, "let us walk in the LORD's light" (2:5). The servant is made "a light for the nations" (42:6; 49:6). Here the nations come to the light of Zion itself, with their kings. Revelation 21:24 applies the words to the holy city: "The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it." In Jewish tradition the chapter is the sixth of the seven haftarot of consolation read after the Ninth of Av (on the Sabbath of Ki Tavo).

a: Raise your eyes and look around you
p: The first half of the verse repeats 49:18 almost word for word; the second recalls 49:22.
b: The Hebrew of "Raise your eyes and look around you: they have all gathered; they are coming to you" is the same as 49:18, and the Plain uses the same words, where Zion, who thought she had lost her children, sees them returning. "Your daughters are carried at the hip", the way a mother carries a small child, recalls 49:22, where the nations carry Zion's sons and daughters home. These chapters often reuse 40–55, and many scholars see the writer of 60–62 as a close reader of that earlier prophecy.

a: the wealth of nations will come to you
p: Chel goyim, "the wealth of the nations", is tribute and trade flowing to Jerusalem.
b: Chel goyim means the riches, even the armies, of the nations (the same phrase returns in 60:11 and 61:6). Ancient capitals received tribute from the peoples they ruled: Assyrian reliefs show foreign envoys bringing goods to the king. Here the flow is reversed in Jerusalem's favor, and the gifts are for the LORD's house (60:7, 13). Haggai 2:7 promises the same: "the treasures of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory". Revelation 21:26 says of the new Jerusalem, "They will bring the glory and honor of the nations into it."

a: carrying gold and frankincense
p: Matthew's magi bring "gold, frankincense and myrrh". Christian art put them on camels from this verse.
b: Midian and Ephah were Arab peoples descended from Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2–4), and Sheba was the kingdom of south Arabia famous for incense and gold (1 Kings 10:1–10). Frankincense is the resin of trees that grow in south Arabia and Somalia, carried north by camel caravans. When the magi bring the child Jesus "gold, frankincense and myrrh" (Matthew 2:11), many readers have heard this verse and Psalm 72:10–11, "May all kings bow down to him". That is why the magi became "kings" with camels in Christian tradition, and why Isaiah 60:1–6 is read at the feast of Epiphany.

a: Every flock of Kedar will be herded to you
p: Two Arab tribes, named in Genesis as sons of Ishmael, bring their flocks for sacrifice.
b: Nebaioth and Kedar were the first two sons of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13), and both were Arab tribes of the north Arabian desert. Assyrian records of the 600s BC name the Qedarites and a people called Nabayati. Some have linked Nebaioth with the later Nabateans of Petra, though the spelling differs and most scholars doubt it. Kedar's black tents and flocks were proverbial (Song of Songs 1:5; Jeremiah 49:28–29). Here the descendants of Ishmael bring rams to the LORD's altar, and they "will go up" and "be accepted", the language of welcome used for foreigners in 56:7.

a: the Tarshish ships first of all
p: Tarshish ships were the large ocean-going traders of the Mediterranean, perhaps named for a port in Spain.
b: Tarshish was a far western port, often identified with Tartessos in southern Spain or with Tarsus in Asia Minor; Jonah tried to sail there to get as far from the LORD as possible (Jonah 1:3). "Ships of Tarshish" came to mean the big merchant ships of the Phoenicians (1 Kings 10:22; Isaiah 2:16; 23:1). Here the fleet that once symbolized human pride carries Zion's children home with silver and gold. "The islands wait for me" repeats 51:5 nearly word for word, and the Plain uses the same English; compare 42:4, where the islands wait for the servant's teaching.

a: Foreigners will build your walls back up
p: Persian kings paid for the rebuilding of the temple. Isaiah pictures foreigners building the walls too.
b: Under Cyrus and Darius, the Persian treasury paid for the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 6:3–8), and Artaxerxes gave Nehemiah timber for the gates and walls (Nehemiah 2:8). The prophet pictures foreigners not just funding but building the walls with their own hands, and their kings serving Zion. The reason is given in God's own words: in fury he struck, but in goodwill he has pitied (compare 54:7–8, "for a brief moment I abandoned you").

a: Your gates will stand open all the time
p: City gates were closed at night and in war. Revelation 21:25 borrows this verse for the new Jerusalem.
b: Walled cities shut their gates at sunset and in danger (Joshua 2:5; Nehemiah 7:3; Nehemiah 13:19). Zion's gates will stand open day and night because no enemy threatens and the gifts never stop coming. Revelation 21:25–26 takes up the verse: "Its gates will never be shut by day, for there will be no night there", and the nations' glory is brought in. "With their kings led in" may mean kings in procession or kings led as captives; the Hebrew nehugim allows both.

a: For the nation and the kingdom that will not serve you will perish
p: Many scholars think this prose-like line was added to the poem. Its tone is harder than its context.
b: The verse breaks the poem's rhythm and speaks of judgment in the middle of a vision of nations coming gladly. Many critical scholars take it as a later comment, perhaps drawing on texts like Zechariah 14:17–19, where nations that do not come up to worship receive no rain. Others read it as part of the poem's point: the new order has one center, and nations that refuse it refuse life. Either way, it reminds the reader that the nations' coming is not just tribute; it is a turning to the LORD.

a: the cypress, the plane tree and the pine together
p: The same three trees appear in 41:19. Their exact identity is uncertain.
b: Berosh, tidhar and te'ashshur are listed together only here and in 41:19, where God plants them in the desert. Berosh is probably a juniper or cypress; the other two are uncertain (elm, plane, pine and box tree have all been proposed). The Plain uses the same names as in 41:19. Lebanon's timber had built Solomon's temple (1 Kings 5:6–10), and Ezra 3:7 says cedar was brought from Lebanon for the second temple. "The place where my feet rest" is the temple, God's footstool (Psalm 132:7, "let us bow low at the footstool for his feet"; compare Isaiah 66:1).

a: will bow at the soles of your feet
p: The children of Zion's oppressors bow before her. Revelation 3:9 turns the image around.
b: The promise repeats 49:23, "Faces to the earth, they will bow to you and lick up the dust of your feet", and 45:14. It is the reversal of exile: those who crushed Zion now honor her as "the City of the LORD". In Revelation 3:9 Jesus tells the small church at Philadelphia that its opponents, "those from the synagogue of Satan", will "come and bow down at your feet. They will know that I have loved you". The image once promised to Zion is given to a persecuted church; readers differ on whether that widens the promise or transfers it.

a: You will suck the milk of nations
p: Kings and nations become Zion's wet nurses: the reversal of 49:23 made physical.
b: In 49:23 kings were to be Zion's "guardians" and their princesses her "wet nurses". Here the picture is bolder: Zion nurses at the breasts of kings. The image says that the nations' strength will feed God's people, as a baby is fed. It returns in 66:11–12, where Jerusalem herself nurses her children. The verse ends with words from 49:26: "I am the LORD, your savior, your redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob", a title from Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:24).

a: In place of bronze I will bring gold
p: Rehoboam replaced Solomon's gold shields with bronze. The new age reverses the decline.
b: When Shishak of Egypt took Solomon's gold shields, "In their place King Rehoboam made shields of bronze" (1 Kings 14:27). Isaiah's list reverses every downgrade: bronze to gold, iron to silver, wood to bronze, stones to iron. The last lines go further. God will make peace Zion's "governor" (pequddah) and righteousness her "taskmaster" (nogesim), the word for Pharaoh's slave drivers (Exodus 3:7; Exodus 5:6) and for the oppressors of 3:12 and 14:2. The only forces that will rule the city are peace and righteousness.
orig: וְשַׂמְתִּי פְקֻדָּתֵךְ שָׁלוֹם וְנֹגְשַׂיִךְ צְדָקָה (vesamti fequddatekh shalom venogsayikh tsedaqah)

a: No longer will the sun be your light by day
p: The LORD himself will be Zion's light. Revelation 21:23 and 22:5 take up the picture.
b: The LORD will replace sun and moon as the city's light, an image of his constant presence. Revelation 21:23 says of the new Jerusalem, "The city does not need the sun or the moon to shine on it, because the glory of God gives it light, and the Lamb is its lamp" (compare Revelation 22:5). Isaiah 24:23 had said that the moon and sun would be ashamed when the LORD reigns on Zion. Whether the prophet meant this literally, as a new creation (65:17), or as a picture of God's presence, readers have long debated. The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek add "by night" (see the variant).

a: Your people will all be righteous
p: The Mishnah's famous teaching that all Israel has a share in the world to come rests on this verse.
b: Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 says: "All Israel have a share in the world to come, as it is said: 'Your people will all be righteous; they will own the land forever...'" The rabbis read "the land" as the world to come and "all righteous" as God's gift to his people, not their own record, though the Mishnah goes on to list those who forfeit their share. The passage is read before each chapter of Pirkei Avot in many synagogues. In context the verse promises a people made righteous and secure in the land, "the sprout of my planting", God's own work. On the Ketiv and Qere of "my planting" see the variant.

a: in its own time I will hurry it on
t: "In its time" and "I will hasten it"
p: The Talmud asked how God can both wait for the right time and hurry. It answered: it depends on Israel.
b: The last line seems to say two things: the promised growth will come "in its time", and God "will hasten it". The Talmud records Rabbi Joshua ben Levi's answer: "If they are worthy, I will hasten it; if they are not worthy, in its time" (Bavli Sanhedrin 98a). The saying became a classic text on the coming of the Messiah: the date is fixed, but repentance can bring it near. Most interpreters read the line more simply: when the time God has set arrives, he will act quickly.

a: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on me
p: An unnamed "me" claims the Spirit and an anointing. Readers have heard the prophet, the servant and Jesus.
b: The speaker is not named. The Targum opens, "The prophet said", and many scholars agree that the prophet of 56–66 here describes his own call, in words drawn from the servant passages: "I have placed my Spirit on him" (42:1), and the servant sent to open blind eyes and free prisoners (42:7; 49:9). Others read the speaker as the servant of the LORD himself, or as a messianic figure; the Spirit rests on the shoot from Jesse in 11:2. In Luke 4:21 Jesus reads the passage in the Nazareth synagogue and says that today this scripture has been fulfilled as they hear it.

a: because the LORD has anointed me
p: Mashach, "anoint", gives the word messiah. Kings and priests were anointed, and once a prophet.
b: Mashach means to smear with oil, and an anointed person is a mashiach, "messiah". Kings (1 Samuel 16:13) and priests (Exodus 28:41) were anointed with oil; Elijah was told to anoint Elisha as prophet (1 Kings 19:16). Cyrus is called the LORD's anointed in 45:1. Here the anointing is with the Spirit rather than oil, and its purpose is to speak: to bring good news. In Greek "anointed" is echrisen, from the same root as Christos, and early Christians heard the verse as a definition of the title Christ (Acts 10:38).

a: to bring good news to the humble
p: Basar, "bring good news", lies behind the Greek euangelion, "gospel". The 'anavim are the humble poor.
b: Lebasser is "to bring good news", the word for the herald running ahead with news of victory (40:9; 52:7; 2 Samuel 18:19–20). The Greek has euangelisasthai, the verb behind "gospel". The 'anavim are the poor and the humble together: people bowed down by poverty and powerless before others (compare 11:4; 29:19). The Greek translates ptōchois, "the poor". Jesus' answer to John the Baptist echoes the line: "the poor are told the good news" (Matthew 11:5), and the first beatitudes may echo 61:1–3 too (Matthew 5:3–4).

a: to proclaim release to the captives
p: Deror is the jubilee word of Leviticus 25:10: the release of slaves and the return of land.
b: Deror is a technical term. In Leviticus 25:10 Israel is told, "Make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim release in the land for all who live in it". Jeremiah 34:8–17 uses the same words for King Zedekiah's release of Hebrew slaves, which the owners soon took back. Babylonian kings also proclaimed release (andurāru) of debts and slaves at the start of a reign. The prophet takes the jubilee as a picture of what God is about to do: the captives go home, debts are cancelled, land returns to its families. The "year of the LORD's goodwill" in 61:2 completes the picture.

a: and an opening wide for those who are bound
p: Peqach-qoach is unusual, perhaps a doubled word: "a wide opening". It is used of opening eyes.
b: Peqach-qoach is written as one word in the Great Isaiah Scroll and as two in the Masoretic Text. Many take it as a doubled form of paqach, "to open": a complete opening. Elsewhere paqach is used only of opening eyes (42:7; 2 Kings 6:17), so the line can mean opening the prison door to the light, or opening blinded eyes, since prisoners were often blinded or kept in darkness (2 Kings 25:7; Isaiah 42:7). The Greek took the second sense and reads "and sight to the blind". Luke follows the Greek (see the variant).

a: to proclaim a year of the LORD's goodwill
p: In Luke 4 Jesus reads to "a year of the Lord's welcome" and rolls up the scroll before "a day of vengeance".
b: Luke 4:18–19 gives the reading in the synagogue at Nazareth. It follows the Greek, adds a line from the Greek of 58:6 (in Luke, "to send the crushed away free"), and ends with "to proclaim a year of the Lord's welcome". Jesus then rolls up the scroll and sits down. He does not read "and a day of our God's vengeance". Many Christian readers have taken this as deliberate: the present time is the time of favor, and judgment belongs to a later day (compare 2 Corinthians 6:2, which quotes Isaiah 49:8). Others note that synagogue readings could end at any point, and that Luke's Jesus speaks of "days of vengeance" later (Luke 21:22). See the chapter page for a fuller comparison.

a: and a day of our God's vengeance
p: Naqam is the act of a ruler setting wrongs right, not a private grudge. It is good news for the oppressed.
b: Naqam is usually translated "vengeance", but in the Bible it is mainly what a lawful ruler does to punish wrong and rescue its victims (Deuteronomy 32:35, 41–43). In 34:8 "a day of vengeance" is a year of recompense for Zion's cause; in 35:4, "Look, your God! Vengeance is coming", he comes to save. The day of vengeance is set beside comfort for those who mourn: the same act frees the oppressed and judges the oppressor. In 63:4 the warrior from Edom says that "a day of vengeance" was in his heart and "the year of my redeemed" had come.

a: to give them a garland instead of ashes
p: Pe'er tachat 'efer: the same letters rearranged. The headdress of joy replaces the ashes of grief.
b: Mourners put ashes or dust on their heads (2 Samuel 13:19; Esther 4:1). The prophet promises them a pe'er, a festive headdress or turban, the same word used of the bridegroom in 61:10 and of a priest's headgear (Exodus 39:28). The Hebrew is a wordplay: pe'er and 'efer use the same three letters. The "oil of rejoicing" is the oil put on the head at feasts instead of being withheld during mourning (2 Samuel 14:2; Psalm 45:7). A "spirit that is faint" is a dim, failing spirit, like the wick in 42:3.

a: People will call them Oaks of Righteousness
p: The people who once worshiped among sacred oaks become oaks themselves, planted by the LORD.
b: In 1:29–30 the people were ashamed of the oaks where they worshiped idols, and they became like an oak whose leaves wither; in 57:5 they burned with lust among the oaks. Now the LORD plants them as 'ele hatsedeq, "oaks of righteousness", strong, long-lived trees, "the LORD's planting, to show his splendor". The planting image ties the verse to 60:21, "the sprout of my planting", and to 61:11, where righteousness sprouts like a garden. The Greek, reading the Hebrew 'ele differently, has "generations of righteousness".

a: But you will be called the priests of the LORD
p: Israel becomes what Exodus 19:6 promised: a kingdom of priests. Revelation says the same of the church.
b: At Sinai God told Israel, "you will be for me a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). The prophet pictures it fulfilled: foreigners do the farming (61:5), and the whole people serve God as priests do, supported by the nations as priests were supported by the tribes (Numbers 18:21). In 66:21, God even takes some foreigners as Levite priests. The New Testament applies the image to believers: "a royal priesthood" (1 Peter 2:9), and in Revelation 1:6 Christ "made us a kingdom and priests to serve his God and Father".

a: Instead of your shame, a double share
p: Mishneh is the firstborn's double portion. Zion, punished double (40:2), now inherits double.
b: Mishneh, "double", can recall the firstborn's inheritance: the father must give the firstborn "a double share of everything he has" (Deuteronomy 21:17). In 40:2 Jerusalem had received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins; now she receives double in blessing. The verse shifts from "your" to "their" in the Masoretic Text, a common movement in Hebrew poetry; the Great Isaiah Scroll smooths it toward "you" in 61:7–9. Zechariah 9:12 uses the same promise: "I will restore to you double".

a: I hate robbery done with crookedness
p: The Hebrew word can also mean "with a burnt offering": the reading of the Talmud, the Vulgate and the KJV.
b: The Masoretic be'olah can be read two ways. 'Olah is a spelling of 'awlah, "injustice" (as in Job 5:16), and the Greek, the Targum ("lying and violence") and most modern translations take it so, matching the line's parallel with justice. The Plain follows that sense. But 'olah is also "burnt offering", and the Vulgate and the KJV ("robbery for burnt offering") read it that way: worship paid for with stolen goods (compare 1:11–15; Malachi 1:13). The Talmud uses that reading to rule that a stolen palm branch may not be used at the festival of Booths, since God hates robbery even in an offering (Bavli Sukkah 30a).

a: I will be full of joy in the LORD
p: The speaker is usually taken as Zion, dressed as a bride. Mary's song in Luke 1 echoes the opening.
b: The speaker changes again. Most readers hear Zion, or the restored people, answering the promises of 61:1–9: "I will be full of joy in the LORD". Some hear the anointed speaker of 61:1 continuing. The opening is close to Habakkuk 3:18 and 1 Samuel 2:1, and Mary's song in Luke 1:46–47 ("My soul declares how great the Lord is, / and my spirit has found its gladness in God my Savior") echoes the same pattern. The Roman Catholic liturgy uses the verse for the Immaculate Conception of Mary, and Jewish tradition reads it as the last of the seven haftarot of consolation (Nitzavim).

a: like a bridegroom who wears his garland like a priest
p: Yekhahen means "he acts as a priest": the groom wears his headdress like a priest's turban.
b: Yekhahen pe'er is literally "he priests a headdress", from kohen, "priest". The bridegroom puts on his festive turban the way the high priest wears his (Exodus 28:4; Exodus 39:28). The image joins wedding and temple: the restored people are both bride and priests (61:6). The Great Isaiah Scroll reads kakkohen, "like a priest", which states the comparison plainly. Many Jewish weddings still crown the bride and groom, and Song of Songs 3:11 speaks of the crown with which Solomon's mother crowned him on his wedding day.

a: For as the earth sends up its shoots
p: Righteousness grows like a garden. The planting image ties 60:21, 61:3 and 61:11 together.
b: The poem ends with a farming picture. Just as the soil sends up shoots and a garden makes seeds sprout, God will make righteousness and praise sprout before the nations. The same verb, tsamach, is used of the "Branch" (tsemach) in Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 3:8, and of righteousness springing up in 45:8: "let the earth open and salvation sprout". The growth is God's work, but it happens openly, in front of all the nations who are watching Zion.

a: Because of Zion I will not keep silent
p: The speaker may be the prophet, refusing to stop praying, or the LORD, who had kept silent too long.
b: The verse does not say who speaks. Many read it as the prophet of 61:1, who will keep speaking and praying for Jerusalem until her vindication shines out; 62:6–7 then calls others to join him. Others hear the LORD himself, who had said in 42:14, "I have said nothing for ages. I kept still; I held myself in", and who in 57:11 and 64:12 is said to keep silent. The same words, "I will not keep silent", return in 65:6. Either way, the verse sets the tone for the chapter: persistent, unashamed speech on Zion's behalf until God acts.

a: A new name will be given you
p: A new name marks a new identity, as with Abraham and Jacob. Revelation promises new names too.
b: In the Bible a new name marks a new status or relationship: Abram becomes Abraham (Genesis 17:5), Jacob becomes Israel (Genesis 32:28). The LORD's "own mouth" will choose Zion's new name, and 62:4 and 62:12 give several. In 65:15 God's servants are promised "another name". Revelation picks up the theme: the victor receives "a white stone ... and written on the stone is a new name" (Revelation 2:17), and the name of the city of my God, "the new Jerusalem" (Revelation 3:12).

a: You will be a beautiful crown in the LORD's hand
p: A crown is usually worn, not held. Zion is the LORD's treasure, held up for others to see.
b: The picture is unexpected: the crown is in God's hand, not on his head. Some think of a royal crown held up to be admired; others of the walled city, since goddesses of cities were shown wearing crowns shaped like city walls, and Jerusalem's walls would be the LORD's crown. The tsenif, "turban", is the royal headdress (compare the priestly turban of Zechariah 3:5). In 28:5 the LORD himself had been "a beautiful crown" for his people; now the people are a crown for him.

a: Instead you will be called My Delight Is in Her
p: The Hebrew names are Hephzibah, "My Delight Is in Her", and Beulah, "Married". Both became English names.
b: Zion's old names were 'Azuvah, "Abandoned", and Shemamah, "Desolate". Her new names are Cheftsi-vah, "My Delight Is in Her", and her land Be'ulah, "Married". The names were real: King Manasseh's mother was "Hephzibah" (2 Kings 21:1), and King Jehoshaphat's mother was "Azubah" (1 Kings 22:42). The KJV kept the Hebrew forms, and both became English names. In John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress the land of Beulah is the peaceful country just before the river of death, and the hymn "Beulah Land" (1876) made the name a picture of heaven. The Greek translated them as "My Will" and "Inhabited".

a: your sons will take you as wife
p: The Hebrew says "your sons" will marry Zion, an awkward picture. Many revocalize to "your builder".
b: The Masoretic Text reads yiv'alukh banayikh, "your sons will marry you". Read as a picture of the land, it means that Zion's children will settle and possess her again, as the Greek understood it ("your sons will dwell in you"). But a son marrying his mother is an odd image beside the bridegroom God in the next line. With different vowels and the same letters, bonayikh means "your Builder", a plural of majesty like the plurals of 54:5, "For your husband is your Maker". Many modern translations adopt that reading. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text (see the variant).

a: With a bridegroom's joy over his bride
p: God rejoices over Zion like a groom on his wedding day. The image runs to the wedding of the Lamb.
b: The prophets often describe the covenant as a marriage: Hosea 2 tells of an unfaithful wife won back, and in 54:5–6 the LORD calls back the wife of his youth. Here the picture is pure joy, without reproach. Zephaniah 3:17 has the same picture: "he will rejoice over you with gladness". The Jewish wedding blessings recall Zion's joy over her children, and in the Gospels Jesus calls himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19–20). Revelation 19:7 announces, "For the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready".
r: 54:5–6; Hosea 2:16–20; Zephaniah 3:17; Jeremiah 33:11; Mark 2:19–20; Revelation 19:7; Revelation 21:2

a: On your walls, Jerusalem, I have posted guards
t: Those who keep the LORD reminded
p: The guards are also mazkirim, "remembrancers", the title of a royal official. Their task is prayer.
b: The guards on the walls never fall silent, day or night. They are then called mazkirim, "those who cause to remember", the title of the royal "recorder" or herald at David's court (2 Samuel 8:16). Their job is to keep reminding God of his promises until he acts. The command "do not rest... and give him no rest" is daring: the people are to pester God, as the widow pesters the judge in Luke 18:1–8. Some Jewish interpreters took the guards as angels, others as prophets or as those who mourn for Zion.

a: The LORD has taken an oath by his right hand
p: The covenant curse said enemies would eat Israel's harvest. God swears that will not happen again.
b: Among the curses of Deuteronomy 28, Israel's enemies would eat the produce of its fields and its labor (Deuteronomy 28:33, 51), and the book of Judges tells of Midianites raiding the harvest (Judges 6:3–6). God now swears by his right hand and his strong arm, the arm that brought Israel out of Egypt, that this will never happen again. The people who sow and gather will eat and drink before the LORD in his courts (62:9), as Deuteronomy commanded for the tithe and firstfruits (Deuteronomy 14:22–26). Compare 65:21–22.

a: Go through, go through the gates!
p: The road-building of 40:3 and 57:14 returns. Now the road leads out through Jerusalem's gates.
b: The commands echo 40:3 ("clear the way of the LORD") and 57:14 ("Heap it up, heap it up, clear the way"), and the Plain uses the same words for the same Hebrew. In chapter 40 the road was for God to come through the desert; here the people are told to go out through the gates and clear the way, perhaps for exiles still returning, or for the nations bringing them home (49:22, where God lifts his flag for the peoples). The doubled verbs give the passage urgency. The Great Isaiah Scroll ends the verse differently (see the variant).

a: Tell Daughter Zion
p: Matthew joins this line with Zechariah 9:9 for Jesus' entry into Jerusalem on a donkey.
b: The message carried to the ends of the earth is for Zion: her salvation is coming, with his reward and his wages going ahead of him, in the same words as 40:10. Matthew's account of Jesus' entry into Jerusalem opens its quotation with this line and continues with Zechariah 9:9: "Tell the daughter of Zion: 'Look, your king is coming to you'" (Matthew 21:5). The Hebrew yish'ekh, "your salvation", is the same root as the name Jesus (Yeshua), and the Greek has "your savior".

a: you will be called Wanted
p: Derushah means "sought after". The city that no one cared about becomes the city everyone seeks.
b: Derushah, "sought out", is the opposite of what Jeremiah 30:17 says Zion's enemies called her: "Zion, no one cares for her" (using the same verb, darash). The chapter ends with four names. The people are "the Holy People" (compare Exodus 19:6, "a holy nation") and "the Redeemed of the LORD" (35:9–10; 51:10). The city is "Wanted" and "A City Not Abandoned", reversing "Abandoned" in 62:4. The KJV's "Sought out" and the Greek's "a city sought after" say the same.

a: Who is this coming in from Edom
t: Edom and Bozrah: red and vintage
p: Edom sounds like 'adom, "red", and Bozrah like batsir, "grape harvest". The names set up the winepress.
b: Edom was Judah's neighbor to the southeast, and Bozrah its chief city. Edom had joined in the fall of Jerusalem (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14), and the prophets made it the symbol of every enemy of God's people (34:5–6; Ezekiel 35). The names carry wordplays. Edom sounds like 'adom, "red", the color of Esau's stew (Genesis 25:30, "That is why he was called Edom"), and of the warrior's clothes. Bozrah sounds like batsir, the grape harvest. In later Jewish writing "Edom" became a code name for Rome, and the passage was read of God's final judgment on Rome.

a: leaning forward in the fullness of his strength
p: Tso'eh usually means "bent over", as a prisoner is. Many scholars change one letter to read "striding".
b: Tso'eh is used in 51:14 of a prisoner bowed down in chains, and the image fits a warrior leaning forward as he marches under the weight of his armor. But many scholars read tso'ed, "striding", by changing one similar letter, and several modern translations adopt it. The Greek has "with force". The Plain keeps the Hebrew, taking it as the forward lean of a strong marcher. The questions of 63:1–2 are like a watchman's challenge at a city gate, and the answer comes in the first person: "It is I".

a: I have trodden the wine trough by myself
p: Grapes were trodden by foot in stone troughs. Revelation 14 and 19 and the "Battle Hymn" take up the image.
b: Grapes were trampled in a purah or gat, a trough cut in rock, and the juice ran into a lower vat. Treading was done by groups, with shouting and song (Jeremiah 25:30; Jeremiah 48:33). This warrior treads alone, and the "grapes" are the peoples. Joel 3:13 uses the same picture of judgment. Revelation 14:19–20 describes "the great winepress of God's anger", and in Revelation 19:15 the rider on the white horse "treads the winepress of the furious anger of God, the Almighty". Julia Ward Howe's "Battle Hymn of the Republic" (1862) sang that the Lord "is trampling out the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored".

a: Their juice spattered on my clothes
p: The juice is the enemies' blood. Many Christian readers have seen Christ's own blood instead.
b: Netsach here means juice or lifeblood, and the text is clear that it is the blood of the trampled peoples. Revelation 19:13 says the rider "wears a robe dipped in blood" before the battle begins, and many interpreters think John meant Christ's own blood, shed on the cross. Early Christian writers often read the whole passage of Christ: Cyprian heard in the red garments the wine of the Lord's blood, and Gregory of Nazianzus read the questions of 63:1 as the angels' question at the ascension. Others insist that the passage is about judgment, not sacrifice, and that the warrior's clothes are stained by others' blood.

a: For a day of vengeance was on my mind
p: The phrase pairs "a day of vengeance" with "the year" of redemption, as 61:2 did.
b: In 61:2 the anointed speaker announced "a year of the LORD's goodwill and a day of our God's vengeance". Here the warrior says that the day of vengeance was in his heart and "the year to redeem my own" (shenat ge'ulay, "the year of my redeemed") had come. In 34:8 the same pairing is used of Edom: "the LORD's day of vengeance, a year of paying back, to win Zion's case". Judgment on the oppressor and rescue of the oppressed are one act. The go'el, the kinsman who redeems, was also the avenger of blood (Numbers 35:19).

a: I looked, and there was no one to help
p: The verse repeats 59:16 almost exactly. The LORD who armed himself there now returns from battle.
b: In 59:16 the LORD looked and "no one was there", and he was shocked that no one stepped in, so his own arm brought him victory. The same Hebrew returns here, with "help" and "held me up". The two passages are bookends around chapters 60–62: in 59 the LORD puts on righteousness as armor and vengeance as clothing (59:17), and in 63 he comes back with his garments stained. Between them stands the vision of Zion's glory. The Plain uses the same wording in both places where the Hebrew agrees.

a: I will call to mind the LORD's acts of loyal love
p: A long prayer begins here (63:7–64:12). Like a lament psalm, it first recalls God's past kindness.
b: The prayer that runs from 63:7 to 64:12 has the shape of a community lament, like Psalms 44, 74, 79 and 89. It opens by remembering the LORD's chasadim, his "acts of loyal love", the plural of hesed (compare Psalm 89:1). Remembering what God has done is the ground for asking him to act again (Psalm 77:11–12). The prayer then tells the story of the exodus and the wilderness (63:8–14), turns to complaint (63:15–19), and ends with confession and plea (64:1–12).

a: In every trouble of theirs, trouble came to him
p: The written Hebrew says "not"; the reading tradition, "to him". The two words sound the same.
b: The Hebrew consonants l' spell the word "not", but the Masoretes read lo, "to him", which sounds the same. With the reading tradition the verse says that in all their distress God himself was distressed: he suffered with his people. This reading is the basis of a famous rabbinic teaching that God shares Israel's exile and suffering. With the written text it says, "in all their distress, he did not distress them" or, joined to the next line as in the Greek, "it was not an envoy or an angel, but he himself saved them". The Plain follows the reading tradition (see the variant).

a: and the angel of his presence saved them
p: Literally "the angel of his face". The Passover Haggadah, like the Greek here, insists God came himself.
b: Mal'akh panav is literally "the messenger of his face". It recalls the angel God sent before Israel (Exodus 23:20) and his promise, "My face will go, and I will give you rest" (Exodus 33:14). Jubilees and later Jewish writings speak of "angels of the presence" who stand before God. The Greek reads differently: "not an envoy nor an angel, but he himself saved them". The Passover Haggadah teaches the same of the exodus: the LORD struck Egypt "I and not an angel, I and not a seraph". The Plain keeps the angel, but the angel stands for God's own presence.

a: and grieved his holy spirit
p: Only here and in Psalm 51:11 does the Hebrew Bible say "holy spirit". Ephesians 4:30 echoes this verse.
b: The phrase ruach qodsho, "his holy spirit", occurs in the Hebrew Bible only in 63:10–11 and Psalm 51:11 ("your holy spirit, do not take it from me"). The rebellion in the wilderness (Psalm 78:40, "How many times they defied him in the wilderness, and caused him pain in the wasteland!") pained God's own spirit, a deeply personal way of speaking. Paul echoes the line: "do not grieve God's holy Spirit" (Ephesians 4:30). Christian readers have seen the passage as an early hint of the Spirit as a person, alongside the Father (63:16) and the angel of his presence (63:9). Jewish readers take the spirit as God's presence and power among his people.

a: with the shepherds of his flock
p: The plural shepherds are Moses and Aaron (Psalm 77:20). The Greek has the singular: Moses.
b: "Where is the one who brought them up out of the sea?" The people remember the crossing of the sea. The Hebrew has "the shepherds of his flock", which most take as Moses and Aaron, perhaps with Miriam (Micah 6:4): "Like sheep you guided your people through Moses and Aaron" (Psalm 77:20). The Greek and some Hebrew manuscripts read "the shepherd", meaning Moses. Hebrews 13:20 calls Jesus "the great shepherd of the sheep" whom God "brought up" from the dead, a phrase that may echo this verse in the Greek.

a: Like a horse in the wilderness
p: A horse runs surely over open country; cattle go down quietly to a valley to graze. Both pictures mean safety.
b: The "wilderness" here is open steppe, where a horse can gallop without stumbling. The people crossed the sea's bed that safely. In 63:14 the image changes to cattle walking down into a valley where there is pasture and water, and "the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest": compare Exodus 33:14, "I will give you rest". The point is God's gentle leading. The whole remembrance (63:11–14) asks, in effect: where is that God now?

a: Look down from heaven and see
p: The plea echoes the prayer at the offering of firstfruits: "Look down from your holy dwelling".
b: Deuteronomy 26:15 gives the prayer said when the tithe was brought: "Look down from your holy dwelling, from the heavens, and bless your people Israel". The plea here borrows its words, but without the offering, because the temple lies in ruins (64:11). "The deep stirring of your heart" is hamon me'eykha, the stirring of the inner parts, the seat of compassion (compare Jeremiah 31:20; Hosea 11:8). The people feel that God has shut that compassion off from them.

a: For you are our Father
p: Calling God "our Father" is rare in the Hebrew Bible. Here and in 64:8 it is the people's strongest plea.
b: God is called Father only a handful of times in the Hebrew Bible (Deuteronomy 32:6, "Isn't he your father?"; Jeremiah 3:4, 19; Malachi 2:10; Psalm 103:13 compares him to one). Here it becomes direct address: "You, LORD, are our Father". Even if Abraham and Israel (Jacob), the ancestors, do not recognize their descendants, God remains their Father and Redeemer. The Jewish prayer Avinu Malkenu, "Our Father, our King", said in the High Holy Days, draws on this language, as does Jesus' prayer, "Our Father, who is in heaven" (Matthew 6:9). Compare 64:8.

a: Abraham does not know us
t: Why would Abraham not know them?
p: Some think of the dead ancestors, who cannot help. Others think of a group excluded by fellow Judeans.
b: The usual reading is that the patriarchs are dead and cannot help, but God, the living Father, can. The Talmud tells a story on this verse: in the age to come God tells Abraham and Jacob that their children have sinned, and they answer, "Let them be wiped out"; only when Isaac pleads do the people turn to God and say, "You are our Father" (Bavli Shabbat 89b). Some modern scholars (Hanson) read a social conflict: a group in Judah felt cut off by those who claimed descent from Abraham and controlled the temple, and appealed past them to God. Others find that reading too specific for a prayer that speaks for all Israel.

a: Why, LORD, do you make us stray from your ways
p: The people blame God for their hard hearts. The prayer is bold, and readers differ on how to take it.
b: The complaint is daring: God has let his people wander and has hardened their hearts. It recalls Isaiah's commission to make the people's heart dull (6:9–10) and the hardening of Pharaoh (Exodus 7:3). Some read it as honest lament, the cry of people who feel abandoned to their sin; others as a statement that God's withdrawal leaves people unable to return without him. Calvin took it as confession that people cannot turn without God's grace; medieval Jewish commentators more often read it as God withholding the help that would have kept them faithful, and so letting their own choice run its course.

a: our foes have trampled your sanctuary
p: The ruined temple of 586 BC is the likeliest event. It gives a date before the temple was rebuilt in 515.
b: The Babylonians burned the temple in 586 BC (some date it 587; 2 Kings 25:8–9). The prayer speaks as though it still lies in ruins, which would place it before the rebuilt temple was dedicated in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15); 64:10–11 says the same.
