The first line is hard: literally "for a little while they possessed your holy people", or, with a slight change, "why have the wicked trampled your holy place?" The Plain takes it as the people's brief possession of the land. Readers who date the passage to Isaiah's time take it as prophetic, seen ahead.

a: If only you would rip open the heavens and come down
p: The cry asks God to tear the sky like cloth. Mark uses the same idea when the heavens split at Jesus' baptism.
b: In Hebrew Bibles this line ends 63:19, so English 64:2–12 is Hebrew 64:1–11 (see the note at 56:1). Qara' means to tear, as a garment is torn in grief (2 Samuel 13:31). The people beg God to rip the sky open and come down as he did at Sinai, when the mountain shook and smoked (Exodus 19:18; Judges 5:4–5; Psalm 18:9). At Jesus' baptism Mark says he "saw the heavens being torn open" and the Spirit coming down (Mark 1:10), with a Greek verb (schizō) that many hear as an answer to this prayer. The Great Isaiah Scroll runs this line straight on from 63:19 with no break.
r: Exodus 19:18; Judges 5:4–5; Psalm 18:9; Psalm 144:5; Micah 1:3–4; Mark 1:10

a: as fire makes water boil
p: Two kitchen images: fire catching dry brushwood and fire bringing a pot to the boil. God's coming is just as sure.
b: The pictures are ordinary ones. Dry brushwood flares up the moment fire touches it, and water heats to boiling over a fire. The people ask God to come with the same speed and certainty, so that his foes would know his name and the nations tremble. The Greek has "as wax melts before fire", an image from Psalm 68:2 and Micah 1:4, where mountains melt at God's coming.

a: no eye has seen a God besides you
p: Paul quotes a saying close to this verse in 1 Corinthians 2:9. Where he found its exact form is debated.
b: Paul writes: "as it is written, What eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and what has not come up into a human heart, all that God has prepared for those who love him" (1 Corinthians 2:9). Paul follows neither the Hebrew ("for those who wait for him") nor the Greek ("for those who wait for mercy"); his "for those who love him" may echo other texts. The line about the heart recalls 65:17, "nor rise up in anyone's heart". Origen said the saying came from a writing he called the Secrets of Elijah (now lost), and Jerome answered that Paul was freely quoting Isaiah. The Gospel of Thomas (saying 17) has a version too. In Isaiah the point is that no other god acts for those who wait for him; Paul turns it toward the hidden wisdom God has given in Christ.

a: We have stayed in them a long time. Will we be saved?
p: The Hebrew here is very uncertain. Translators have guessed widely; the Greek reads "therefore we went astray".
b: Word for word the line reads "in them forever, and we will be saved". "In them" may mean "in our sins" or "in your ways" (64:5a); "forever" may mean "for a long time"; and "we will be saved" may be a question or a statement. The KJV has "in those is continuance, and we shall be saved". Many modern scholars think the text was damaged early and correct it in different ways. The Plain takes it as a question that fits the lament: after so long in sin, can we be saved? The Greek reads "therefore we went astray" (see the variant).

a: and like a cloth from a woman's monthly period are all our right deeds
p: Beged 'iddim is a cloth used during menstruation. The law counted it unclean; the KJV called it "filthy rags".
b: Beged 'iddim is literally "a garment of periods": a cloth used during a woman's monthly bleeding. The Torah treated such blood as making a person and her cloths ritually unclean for a time (Leviticus 15:19–24), so the image means something that cannot be brought near the holy. It says nothing against women or their bodies. The Greek has "a rag of a woman sitting apart", and the KJV made the phrase famous as "filthy rags". The people say that even their acts of righteousness are unclean, because the whole community is unclean ("like someone unclean", the cry of Leviticus 13:45).

a: We wither like a leaf, all of us
p: Sin makes the people wither like leaves, and their wrongdoing blows them away like the wind.
b: The image is autumn. A withered leaf is light and dry, and the wind carries it away (compare 1:30; 40:7–8; Psalm 1:4). In 40:6–8 all flesh is grass and its beauty a flower that withers, but the word of God stands forever. Here the people apply the picture to themselves: it is their own wrongdoing that is the wind. The line moves the confession from uncleanness to frailty: they are both unfit to approach God and unable to stand.

a: No one calls on your name
t: No one takes hold of God
p: To "take hold" of God (hachaziq) is to cling to him in prayer. No one does, because God has hidden his face.
b: The verse describes a circle. No one prays or "stirs himself to take hold" of God (the verb is used in 27:5 of taking hold of God's protection, and in 56:2, 4, 6 of holding fast to the covenant). Yet the reason given is that God has hidden his face, so they melt away in their sins. The Greek, the Targum and the Syriac read "you handed us over" to our sins (see the variant), a phrase Paul uses of God's judgment in Romans 1:24–28.

a: We are the clay, and you are the one who shaped us
p: The potter image warned against arguing with God in 29:16 and 45:9. Here the people use it to plead with him.
b: Elsewhere the potter image is a rebuke: the clay cannot question the potter (29:16; 45:9, "Does the clay say to the one who shapes it, 'What are you making?'"; compare Jeremiah 18:1–6 and Romans 9:20–21). In this prayer it becomes an argument for mercy. We are clay; you shaped us; we are all your handiwork, so you cannot abandon what you made. It is joined to the second "our Father" of the prayer (63:16). Compare Job 10:9: "Please remember: you shaped me as from clay."
orig: אֲנַחְנוּ הַחֹמֶר וְאַתָּה יֹצְרֵנוּ ('anachnu hachomer ve'attah yotserenu)

a: The cities of your holiness lie as open wilderness
p: Judah's towns and Jerusalem are a wilderness, and the temple has burned. The picture fits the years after 586 BC.
b: The Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and many towns of Judah in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8–10; Jeremiah 34:7), and archaeology shows that much of the land was thinly settled for decades. The prayer calls Judah's towns "cities of your holiness", because the land belongs to God. The temple where "our ancestors praised you" has been burned (64:11). The scene matches Lamentations, especially Lamentations 1:4 and 5:18, and it is one reason most scholars date this prayer before the temple was rebuilt.

a: Will you keep silent and crush us beyond all bounds?
p: The lament ends with a question, like Lamentations. God's answer comes in 65:1: "I let myself be found".
b: The prayer ends without resolution, with the verb of 42:14 ("I have said nothing for ages") and 62:1 ("I will not keep silent"). Lamentations also ends on a question: "unless you have utterly rejected us?" (Lamentations 5:22). In the book as it now stands, God answers in the next verse: "I let myself be asked by those who did not ask" (65:1). Many scholars think chapter 65 was written or placed as a reply to this lament.

a: I let myself be asked by those who did not ask
t: Found by those who did not look
p: God answers the lament: he was ready to be found. Paul applied the verse to the Gentiles.
b: The verbs say that God "let himself be sought" and "let himself be found": he was always available, even to people who did not ask. In context the verse answers the prayer of 63:7–64:12, which complained that God was silent; God replies that it is his people who have not sought him (65:2–7). Paul reads it differently in Romans 10:20: "I was found by those not seeking me; I became visible to those not asking for me", which he applies to the Gentiles, and the next verse to Israel. Jewish and many modern readers keep both verses about Israel.

a: I have spread out my hands all day long
p: God holds out his hands like someone pleading. Early Christians saw the arms of Christ on the cross.
b: To spread out the hands is a gesture of prayer (1 Kings 8:22) or of appeal to someone. Here God is the one appealing, all day, to a people who walk their own way. Paul quotes it in Romans 10:21: "All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people who disobey and talk back", following the Greek. Early Christian writers, among them the Letter of Barnabas (12:4), Justin and Irenaeus, saw in the outstretched hands a picture of Jesus on the cross, holding out his arms to the people.

a: sacrificing in the gardens
p: Garden worship is condemned in 1:29 and 66:17. Brick altars broke the law for altars of earth or uncut stone.
b: Sacred gardens or groves were places of worship for other gods or for the LORD in forbidden forms (1:29; 66:17). "Making smoke on the bricks" may mean burning incense on brick altars or on roofs made of tiles, as in Jeremiah 19:13 and 32:29. The law allowed altars of earth or of uncut stone only (Exodus 20:24–25). The Greek adds "to demons, which do not exist". The Great Isaiah Scroll has an obscure reading here: perhaps "they suck hands on the stones" (see the variant).

a: who sit among the tombs
p: Spending the night among tombs was a way to consult the dead. The Greek says they slept there "for dreams".
b: Sitting among tombs and passing the night in "hidden places" (perhaps caves or guarded sites) points to rites for contacting the dead, forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:11 (compare Isaiah 8:19; 57:9). The Greek adds that they lie there "for dreams", the practice of sleeping at a holy site to receive a vision. Pork was forbidden ("It is unclean for you", Leviticus 11:7), and pigs were sacrificed in some foreign cults; in 167 BC Antiochus IV ordered Jews "to sacrifice pigs and unclean animals" (1 Maccabees 1:47). Mark's story of the man who lived among the tombs, near a herd of pigs, recalls this verse (Mark 5:1–13).

a: for I would make you holy
p: The KJV's "holier than thou" became an English idiom. The Hebrew says, "I would make you holy".
b: Qedashtikha means "I have made you holy" or "I would make you holy". The people who perform these rites tell others to keep away, since contact with their holiness would pass it on, the way touching the altar made a thing holy (Exodus 29:37; Ezekiel 44:19; Haggai 2:12). The KJV translated, "I am holier than thou", and the phrase became the English name for self-righteousness. God says such people are smoke in his nose, an irritation that never goes away. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "do not touch me" for "do not come near me".

a: paid it back into their lap
p: The lap (cheq) is the fold of a robe used as a pocket. Payment poured into it is full and close at hand.
b: The cheq is the fold of the robe above the belt, where people carried grain or goods (Ruth 3:15; Luke 6:38). To pay "into the lap" is to pay in full, directly to the person. Psalm 79:12 prays, "Repay our neighbors sevenfold, right into their laps". "It is written down in front of me" pictures a record kept before God, like the books of judgment in Daniel 7:10 and Revelation 20:12. God will not keep silent (compare 62:1; 64:12) but will pay back.

a: 'Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,'
p: A vintage saying about a good cluster in a poor vine. The words are also a tune name in four psalm titles.
b: At the grape harvest, someone finds a cluster with juice in it and says, "Do not destroy it, there is a blessing in it": perhaps a line from a vintage song. In the same way God will not destroy the whole people for the sake of his servants, the good grapes in a bad vine (compare the vineyard of 5:1–7). 'Al tashchitehu, "Do not destroy", is close to the heading of Psalms 57, 58, 59 and 75 ("On 'Do Not Destroy'"), probably the name of a tune. The idea is the remnant: a holy seed kept in a judged people (6:13; 10:20–22).

a: The Sharon will become a pasture for sheep
p: Sharon is the coastal plain in the west; the Valley of Achor lies near Jericho in the east. All the land will flourish.
b: The Sharon is the fertile coastal plain between Joppa and Mount Carmel (35:2; Song of Songs 2:1). The Valley of Achor, near Jericho, was named for Achan's sin and the "great heap of stones" over him (Joshua 7:24–26); Hosea 2:15 promised that it would become "a door of hope". Together the two names cover the land from west to east. Places of trouble become pasture, "for my people who have looked for me", the opposite of those in 65:1 who did not look.

a: who lay out a table for Luck
p: Gad ("Luck") and Meni ("Fate") were gods of fortune. Meals were set out for gods to share.
b: Gad was a god of good fortune known across the Levant; place names such as Baal-gad (Joshua 11:17) and Migdal-gad preserve it, and Aramaic and Phoenician inscriptions mention him. Meni (Meni, "Fate" or "Portion") may be related to Manat, a goddess of destiny worshiped later in Arabia, but this is uncertain. Ancient worshipers set tables of food and mixed wine for gods as a shared meal. The Greek reads "the demon" and "Fortune" (Tyche); the KJV has "that troop" and "that number". The next verse puns on Meni: "I will make the sword your fate" (maniti).

a: For I called, and you did not answer
p: The same words return in 66:4. The people complained that God was silent; God says they were deaf.
b: The four lines "For I called, and you did not answer; I spoke, and you did not listen. You did what is evil in my eyes and chose what I do not want" are repeated almost exactly in 66:4, and the Plain uses the same words in both places. Compare 50:2, "Why, when I called, was there no one to answer?" The lament of chapter 64 accused God of hiding his face and keeping silent; the answer is that he called and they did not answer. The verse sets up the reversal of 65:24, where God answers before his servants call.

a: Look, my servants will eat
p: Chapters 65–66 divide God's people into "my servants" and those who forsake him. Who were the two groups?
b: In 40–55 "my servant" is Israel, or one figure who serves for Israel. In 65–66 the word is plural, "my servants", and it marks one group within the people, set against "you who abandon the LORD" (65:11). The blessings and woes of 65:13–14 are like those of Luke 6:20–26. Some scholars (Hanson) see a real conflict between a prophetic group and the priests who ran the rebuilt temple; others (Schramm) see the dispute as about traditional religion and foreign worship. Many readers simply take it as the old line between the faithful and the faithless.

a: You will leave your name behind
p: "The Lord GOD will kill you" may be God's own statement or the curse people will say. The Plain takes it as the curse.
b: To leave a name "as a curse word" means that people will use it in curse formulas, as in Jeremiah 29:22: "May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire". The Hebrew vehemitkha Adonai YHWH can be read simply as God's statement, "and the Lord GOD will put you to death", as the KJV and most versions take it. It can also be the words of the curse itself, as the Jewish Publication Society's translation takes it, and the Plain follows that reading. In contrast, God's servants will be called by "another name", as Zion received a new name in 62:2. Revelation 2:17 and 3:12 take up the new name. The Great Isaiah Scroll ends the curse with "forever" and lacks the last line (see the variant).

a: will ask it by the God of Amen
p: Amen means "firm" or "true". The Greek has "the true God", and in Revelation 3:14 Christ is "the Amen".
b: 'Elohe 'amen, "the God of Amen", occurs only here. Amen comes from the root for firmness and faithfulness: it is what people say to confirm a blessing or an oath (Numbers 5:22; Deuteronomy 27:15–26). God is the one whose word is sure. The Greek has "the true God"; the Latin Vulgate keeps the word (in Deo amen). Revelation 3:14 calls Christ "the Amen, the faithful and true witness", and Paul says that all God's promises find their "yes" and their "amen" in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). Some scholars revocalize to 'omen, "faithfulness".

a: For look, I am creating new heavens and a new earth
t: New heavens and a new earth
p: The verb is bara', "create", the word of Genesis 1:1. Revelation 21:1 and 2 Peter 3:13 take up the promise.
b: Bara', "create", is used in the Bible only with God as subject; it opens Genesis: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). Here God is creating them anew. The next verse narrows the focus: "I am creating Jerusalem to be a joy". Some read the promise as a renewal of the whole world, others as poetry for a transformed Jerusalem and its life. 2 Peter 3:13 says, "we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness lives, as he promised", and Revelation 21:1 sees "a new heaven and a new earth". The past "will not be remembered": compare 43:18–19.
orig: כִּי־הִנְנִי בוֹרֵא שָׁמַיִם חֲדָשִׁים וָאָרֶץ חֲדָשָׁה (ki-hineni vore' shamayim chadashim va'arets chadashah)

a: The sound of weeping and the sound of crying out
p: The promise returns in Revelation 21:4: "Death will be gone, and grief and crying and pain will be gone too".
b: God himself will rejoice over Jerusalem (compare 62:5) and the city will hear no more weeping or cries for help. In 25:8 God "will wipe away tears from all faces" and swallow up death. Revelation 21:4 joins the two promises: "He will wipe every tear out of their eyes. Death will be gone, and grief and crying and pain will be gone too. The first things have gone away". Isaiah's picture still includes death at a great age (65:20); Revelation's does not.

a: For whoever dies at a hundred will die young
p: In the new Jerusalem people live long, but they still die. Readers differ on what age this describes.
b: The verse promises an end to infant death and to lives cut short. A person who dies at a hundred will be thought a youth, and one who "falls short" of a hundred (hachote', "the one who misses", usually "the sinner") will be counted as cursed. Death and sin are still present. Dispensationalist and premillennial readers see here the thousand-year reign of Revelation 20, before the final new creation. Amillennial readers take it as a picture of the eternal state in the language of this world. Many critical scholars read it as an idealized life in a restored Jerusalem. See the traditions card.
orig: וְהַחוֹטֶא בֶּן־מֵאָה שָׁנָה יְקֻלָּל (vehachote' ben-me'ah shanah yequllal)

a: They will build houses and live in them
p: The covenant curse said others would live in the houses Israel built. Now those who build will live in them.
b: Deuteronomy 28:30 warned: "You will build a house and never live there. You will plant a vineyard and never get to use its grapes." The promise reverses the curse: the people will enjoy the work of their own hands (compare 62:8–9; Amos 9:14). Their lives will be "like the lifetime of a tree": in the ancient world trees such as the oak, olive or terebinth could live for centuries. The Greek reads "like the days of the tree of life", recalling the tree of life in Eden (Genesis 2:9), and the Targum does too, linking the promise to Eden.

a: Even before they call, I will answer
p: The people's complaint that God did not answer (64:12) and God's that they did not answer (65:12) both end here.
b: The chapter has moved from a people who did not call on God's name (64:7; 65:1) and a God whose call went unanswered (65:12) to a time when God answers before anyone calls. The promise reverses the silence of the lament on both sides. Jesus says something similar about prayer: "Your Father knows the things you have need of before you ever ask him" (Matthew 6:8). Compare 58:9: "Then you will call, and the LORD will answer".

a: The wolf and the lamb will graze together
p: The verse sums up 11:6–9, Isaiah's vision of peace among animals, and adds the snake's curse from Genesis.
b: Chapter 11 pictured peace in the creation under the shoot of Jesse: "The wolf will stay as a guest with the lamb... the lion, like the ox, will eat straw... No one will hurt or ruin anything anywhere on my holy mountain" (11:6–9). This verse repeats it in shortened form, using the same Hebrew for the lion and for the last lines, and the Plain uses the same words as 11:7 and 11:9. It adds "dust will be the snake's food", from the curse in Genesis 3:14 ("dust you will eat all the days of your life"): the snake is left humbled, and nothing harmful remains. Popular art often calls it "the lion and the lamb", though neither passage pairs them.

a: the earth is the stool for my feet
t: Heaven a throne, earth a footstool
p: Jesus forbids swearing by the earth, "since it is the stool for his feet". Stephen quotes the verse in Acts 7.
b: The ark in the temple was called God's footstool (Psalm 132:7; 1 Chronicles 28:2). Here the whole earth is his footstool, and no house can hold him; Solomon had said the same at the temple's dedication: "the heavens above the heavens, are not big enough for you. Then how could this house I built be enough!" (1 Kings 8:27). Jesus forbids swearing "by the earth, since it is the stool for his feet" (Matthew 5:35). In Acts 7:48–50 Stephen quotes this verse almost word for word from the Greek ("what kind of house will you build me... or what is the place of my rest?") to argue that "the Most High does not live in houses made by hands", a speech that led to his death.

a: Where then is the house that you would build for me?
p: Does God reject the rebuilding of the temple, or only the idea that a building could contain him?
b: Some scholars read this as opposition to the temple rebuilt in 520–515 BC, which Haggai urged on the people (Haggai 1:2–11): God does not want a house at all. Most read it as a warning against trusting a building, as Jeremiah did (Jeremiah 7:4): the same chapter speaks of the temple (66:6) and of offerings brought to the LORD's house (66:20). The next verse shows what God looks for: "the poor one, stricken in spirit, who trembles at my word". Jewish commentators such as Radak read it as God's freedom from any place, and Christian readers, with Stephen, as pointing beyond the temple.

a: who trembles at my word
p: Chared, "trembling", gave its name to the Haredi Jews of today. Ezra's supporters were "those who tremble".
b: Chared 'al-devari, "trembling at my word", describes someone in awe of God's word, who takes it with deep seriousness. The phrase returns in 66:5. In Ezra 9:4, "All who trembled at what the God of Israel had said" gathered to Ezra, and in Ezra 10:3 "those who tremble at our God's command" back his reform. The modern word Haredi (plural Haredim), used for strictly Orthodox Jews, comes from these verses. God's gaze rests not on a building but on the poor ('ani) and "stricken in spirit" (compare 57:15).

a: One who slaughters an ox, one who kills a man
p: The Hebrew sets two acts side by side without a verb. They may be compared ("is like") or simply joined.
b: The verse pairs a lawful sacrifice with a horror: one who slaughters an ox, one who kills a man; one who sacrifices a lamb, one who breaks a dog's neck; grain offering, pig's blood; incense, idol-blessing. The Hebrew gives no verb. Most translations since the KJV supply "is like": a sacrifice offered by such people is as bad as murder. Others read it as describing people who do both at once, mixing temple worship with pagan rites. The Plain keeps the Hebrew's bare pairing. The Great Isaiah Scroll's "like one who strikes" supports the comparison (see the variant). Breaking a neck was the law's way of killing an unransomed donkey (Exodus 13:13); dogs were unclean.

a: who push you out because of my name
p: Menaddekhem, "those who push you out", later gave the word niddui, the synagogue ban.
b: The faithful who tremble at God's word are hated and excluded by their own "brothers". The verb nadah, "push away", became in later Hebrew the word for niddui, the ban that excluded a person from the community (compare Amos 6:3). The mockers say, "Let the LORD show his glory, so we can see your joy!", scorning their hope. Jesus warned his followers that they would be put out of the synagogue for his name (John 16:2). Some scholars see in this verse the conflict between the prophet's group and the temple leadership.

a: Before she was in labor, she gave birth
p: Zion bears a nation in a day, without labor pains. Revelation 12 reverses the picture.
b: The image is a miracle: Zion gives birth before her pains start, and a whole nation is born "in one day". In 26:17–18 the people had been in labor and given birth to wind; in 54:1 the barren woman was told to sing. Now the population of Zion appears suddenly. The "boy" stands for the people as a whole (66:8, "her sons"). Revelation 12 uses a related picture: a woman "cried out in pain as she was about to give birth", and "She gave birth to a son, a male child, who is going to rule all the nations" (Revelation 12:2, 5). The Targum renders the end of the verse "her king will be revealed", and Genesis Rabbah 85:1 reads it of the final redeemer, born before Israel's first oppressor.

a: Like someone whose mother comforts him
p: God compares himself to a mother comforting her child. The Bible's images of God are not only male.
b: Jerusalem is first the nursing mother (66:11–12), and then God himself takes the mother's place: "so I myself will comfort you". Isaiah uses such images more than any other book: God cries out like a woman in labor (42:14) and cannot forget her nursing child (49:15). The word "comfort" ties the end of the book to its turning point, "Comfort, comfort my people" (40:1). Theologians from Anselm to Julian of Norwich drew on images like this one when they spoke of God's motherly care.

a: For look, the LORD will come in fire
p: Fire and storm chariots are the signs of God's coming in judgment, as at Sinai and in the Psalms.
b: God comes "in fire" with "chariots like the storm wind", the imagery of the divine warrior (Psalm 68:17, "God's chariots are twenty thousand"; Habakkuk 3:8). Fire marked his presence at Sinai (Exodus 19:18) and the chariot of fire took Elijah up (2 Kings 2:11). The verse looks back to the warrior of 59:15–20 and 63:1–6. In 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8 Paul speaks of the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven "in flaming fire", in words close to the Greek of this verse.

a: following one in the middle
p: A leader of the rite stands in the middle of the garden. The written and read Hebrew differ on "one".
b: The rite is in sacred gardens (65:3), with people purifying themselves to follow "one in the middle": perhaps a priest or leader at the center, perhaps an image of a god. The written text has the masculine "one" ('echad), the reading tradition the feminine ('achat), which some take as a goddess (see the variant). The foods are forbidden: pork, "vile things" (sheqets, swarming creatures) and the mouse ("the weasel, the mouse", Leviticus 11:29). Ezekiel 8:7–12 describes a secret rite in the temple with seventy elders and a leader "standing among them".

a: As for me, I know their deeds and their thoughts
p: The Hebrew says only, "And I, their deeds and their thoughts". The verb has to be supplied.
b: Literally the verse begins "And I, their deeds and their thoughts, it is coming to gather all nations". A verb seems to be missing. The KJV supplied "For I know their works and their thoughts", and the Plain does the same. Some join the words to the previous verse ("I [will punish] their deeds"); the Greek reads "I am coming to gather". The verse then turns from judgment to the nations: God will gather "all nations and languages" to see his glory, a reversal of the scattering at Babel (Genesis 11:9) and an image taken up at Pentecost (Acts 2:5–11).

a: to Tarshish, Pul and Lud, who draw the bow
p: Most names come from the table of nations in Genesis 10. They mark the edges of the known world.
b: Tarshish lay in the far west (60:9). "Pul" is probably Put, in Libya, as the Greek reads (Genesis 10:6, "Cush, Mizraim, Put and Canaan"); Lud may be Lydia in Asia Minor or a people of Africa (Genesis 10:13). "Who draw the bow" may be Meshech, as the Greek has it (Genesis 10:2, "Javan, Tubal, Meshech"). Tubal was in eastern Asia Minor, and Javan is Ionia, the Greeks. The survivors God sends out to these peoples "will tell of my glory among the nations", one of the clearest pictures in the Hebrew Bible of messengers sent out to the nations. Some scholars think the list shaped Paul's plan to reach Spain (Romans 15:24).

a: They will bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD
p: The nations bring Israel's scattered people home as a grain offering. Paul speaks of "the offering of the Gentiles".
b: The nations escort "your brothers", the scattered Israelites, to Jerusalem on every kind of transport, and the returning people are themselves the offering, brought like grain in a clean vessel. The picture continues 49:22 and 60:4, 9. Paul describes his mission in temple language: he serves "so that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable, made holy by the Holy Spirit" (Romans 15:16). Many scholars think he had this verse in mind, though for Paul the Gentiles themselves are the offering.

a: And I will take some of them too to be Levite priests
p: Does "some of them" mean foreigners from the nations, or returning Israelites? The sentence allows both.
b: "Them" could be the nations who bring the exiles (66:19–20), or the exiles who are brought. If it is the nations, the verse is astonishing: foreigners would serve as priests, which the law reserved for Aaron's descendants (Numbers 3:10; Numbers 18:7). The book would end where 56:6–7 began, with foreigners ministering at God's altar. Many modern scholars take it this way. Others, including Rashi, read it of Israelites from the diaspora, whose priestly descent was lost or unknown (compare Ezra 2:61–63). The Hebrew has "to priests, to Levites", without "and" (see the variant).

a: For just as the new heavens and the new earth
p: The new heavens and earth of 65:17 return. The people's name will last as long as the new creation.
b: The promise of 65:17 returns in a new role: as surely as the new heavens and earth will stand, so will Israel's descendants and name. The verb "stand" ('amad) is used of God's word in 40:8, "the word of our God stands forever". Jeremiah 31:35–36 makes a similar pledge from the fixed order of sun, moon and stars. Compare the eunuchs of 56:5, who were promised "a name better than sons and daughters".

a: From new moon to new moon
p: "All flesh" will worship at the feasts of the calendar. The Mishnah read the verse of judgment lasting a year.
b: New moons and Sabbaths were the regular feasts of Israel's calendar (1:13–14; Numbers 28:9–15; Amos 8:5). In the future all humanity will come to worship on them, as Zechariah 14:16 has the nations come up for the feast of booths. The Greek adds "in Jerusalem" (see the variant). The Mishnah used this verse in a debate about how long the wicked are judged: Rabbi Akiva said the judgment of the wicked in Gehenna lasts twelve months, from one new moon to the same new moon a year later; Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri read "from Sabbath to Sabbath" as the seven weeks from Passover to Shavuot (Mishnah Eduyot 2:10).

a: For their worm will not die
t: The worm that does not die
p: The corpses of the rebels lie outside the city. Jesus quotes the verse of Gehenna in Mark 9:48.
b: The worshipers leave the city and see the bodies of those who rebelled, consumed by worms and fire that do not stop. The picture is of corpses outside Jerusalem, perhaps in the Valley of Hinnom, where Josiah had defiled the child-sacrifice site (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–33). The valley's name became Gehenna, the place of final punishment. Jesus warns of being thrown "into Gehenna, where their worm never dies and the fire is never put out" (Mark 9:47–48), in words close to the Greek of this verse, turned into the present tense. Judith 16:17 says of the nations, "He will put fire and worms into their flesh, and they will weep and feel it forever".
orig: כִּי תוֹלַעְתָּם לֹא תָמוּת (ki tola'tam lo' tamut)
r: 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–33; Mark 9:43–48; Judith 16:17; Matthew 25:41; Revelation 14:10–11

a: and they will be a horror to all flesh
p: Dera'on, "horror", occurs only here and in Daniel 12:2. Synagogues repeat 66:23 so as not to end on it.
b: Dera'on, "abhorrence", is used elsewhere only in Daniel 12:2, where some of those who sleep in the dust awake to everlasting life, and others "to shame and everlasting abhorrence". That link made Isaiah's verse a text about the fate of the wicked after death. Because the book ends so harshly, Jewish practice is to read 66:23 again after 66:24 when the chapter is read in the synagogue, so that the reading ends with worship. The same is done at the end of the Twelve Prophets, Lamentations and Ecclesiastes. Printed Hebrew Bibles often repeat the verse in small type.
